label: Person
name: Albert Gregory Meyer
summary:
Albert Gregory Meyer (1903–1965) was an American cardinal and Archbishop of Chicago who played a decisive role at the Second Vatican Council as one of the most influential advocates for progressive reform. Born in Milwaukee, he was ordained a priest in 1926 and rose through the American hierarchy, becoming Archbishop of Milwaukee in 1953 and Archbishop of Chicago in 1958 before being elevated to cardinal in 1959.

At Vatican II, Meyer was a member of the council's Central Preparatory Commission and emerged as one of the American hierarchy's most eloquent voices for the reformist agenda. His interventions in council debates—delivered in polished Latin—were consistently among the most theologically rigorous, addressing religious freedom, ecumenism, the nature of the Church, and the relationship between Scripture and Tradition. He worked closely with Cardinals Döpfner, Suenens, and other progressive leaders, and his premature death from a brain tumour in April 1965 (three months before the council's final session) deprived the American Church of one of its most capable council advocates.

Meyer's most significant single contribution may have been his dramatic intervention in the final session before his illness, supporting the Declaration on Religious Freedom (Dignitatis Humanae) when it was threatened with a procedural delay. His public support, along with other American cardinals, helped prevent its suppression. His death was mourned as a significant loss for the council's final work.
